title: runtime-qualification-circuit-and-chaos-lab-manual-2026
author: Priya Desai
content:
Runtime qualification circuit and chaos lab — manual

Purpose
This document defines the standard experimental qualification circuit we use to validate changes to the serving runtime surface (kernel patches, scheduler policy changes, fallback routing, KV cache logic, and runtime config knobs). It pairs structured benchmarks with deterministic and stochastic chaos experiments and provides a single, reproducible gating checklist for releases.

Scope
- Applies to any code or config change that affects: kernel selection/execution, request scheduling/admission, KV cache behaviour, batching/packing logic, or telemetry/trace collection paths.
- Includes both pre-merge CI sanity tests and staged canary/qualification runs in the chaos lab.

Outcome and acceptance criteria (high level)
- No P0 regressions in production SLOs during the canary window: 99th percentile tail latency ≤ pre-change baseline + 15% and p75 ≤ baseline + 8%.
- Resource efficiency: per-token GPU micros (measured by kernel-time-trace) must not exceed baseline by more than +12% for default load shapes unless feature flagged (requires business signoff).
- Quality / fidelity: when applicable, outputs must pass the regression prompt set acceptance suite with zero critical regressions.
- Observability contract: all new signals introduced by the change must be emitted and documented before rollout.

Qualification circuit: phases and expected artifacts
1) Local dev and unit-level profiling
   - Fast path: run microbenchmarks from the repo /bench/local and the kernel unit harness. Capture single-GPU kernel latencies and memory footprints.
   - Artifacts: kernel latency CSV, memory allocation timeline, and a short explanatory note.

2) CI integration smoke and deterministic benchmark
   - CI runs the integration harness that replays a fixed request corpus (low-entropy synthetic + replayed production traces) across the runtime in a containerized fixture.
   - Pass/fail gates: no increased assertion failures, no trace reordering, and a per-test latency regression threshold.

3) Chaos-lab qualification (isolated cluster)
   - Target: a dedicated qualification cluster (tag: chaos-qualifier) sized to match the smallest production cluster.
   - Runbook steps (numbered):
     1. Deploy change to 5% of nodes behind a controlled load generator.
     2. Run the benchmark harness (see Benchmarks below) under three traffic shapes: steady, burst, and mixed latency-sensitive.
     3. Inject deterministic kernel perturbations: add a synthetic 10–50ms delay in the slowest attention kernel and verify scheduler hedging/timeout behaviour.
     4. Run stochastic chaos phases: network partitions (0.5–2s jitter), NVMe fault injection (simulated stalls), and transient GPU throttling simulation.
     5. Monitor telemetry dashboard (Latency, Error-rate, Kernel-queue-depth, GPU-utilization) and the qualification acceptance checklist.
   - Artifacts: full benchmark results, crash dumps, kernel traces, and an incident-style summary for any anomaly.

4) Canary + rollback validation (production-but-controlled)
   - Canary window: 24–72 hours depending on change size and risk profile.
   - Traffic steering: start with 1% of traffic, progress to 10% only if all SLOs and checks pass at each step.
   - Rollforward rules: automatic at each step if: (a) no P0 signals for 2h, (b) error-rate delta < 0.1% absolute, and (c) tail latency within acceptance bound.
   - Automatic rollback triggers: error-rate > 3x baseline for 15 minutes, p99 latency > baseline + 50% for 10 minutes, OR any kernel watchdog crash.

Benchmarks and test corpus (what to run)
- Baseline corpora:
  - small-chat: median length 60 tokens, mostly streaming, latency-sensitive.
  - long-completion: median length 1,200 tokens, throughput focused.
  - multi-turn-chat: mixes prefix cache reuse patterns to exercise KV cache.
- For each corpus run: record per-token kernel time, scheduler queue metrics, GPU occupancy, and memory high-water marks.
- Statistical reporting: p50/p75/p95/p99/p999 for latency; mean and 95% CI for per-token kernel micros.

Profiles and telemetry required
- Mandatory telemetry emitted during qualification run:
  - kernel.exec_time_ms (per-kernel tag), kernel.exec_count, kernel.queue_depth
  - request.latency_ms (per-stage: queue, kernel, postprocess), request.path (route tag), request.trace_id
  - gpu.utilization_pct, gpu.memory_used_mb, gpu.temp_celsius
  - kvcache.hit_ratio_prefix, kvcache.hot_evictions, kvcache.repopulation_latency_ms
- Tagging: all metrics for a qualification run must include qualifier_id and experiment_label.

Observability & dashboards
- Create a temporary dashboard for each qualification run that includes:
  - Time-series for p99 tail latency, request error-rate, kernel queue depth heatmap, and GPU memory pressure.
  - A waterfall view (textual) of the top 5 slow requests with kernel traces attached.
- Logging: increase kernel-level debug logging only for the qualification run (env var RK_QUAL_DEBUG=true) and ensure logs are retained for 14 days in the qualification workspace.

Experiment catalogue (example matrix)
- The following table (described) maps experiment types to goals and pass criteria:
  - kernel-change | goal: ensure no kernel-time regressions; pass: p99 per-kernel exec_time <= baseline * 1.12
  - scheduler-policy | goal: preserve tail SLOs under mixed load; pass: tail latency + queued requests within budget and no starvation events
  - kvcache-tuning | goal: reduce median latency for multi-turn; pass: prefix hit_ratio increases by >=10% without >5% memory overhead
  - tracing-addition | goal: increase observability; pass: all traces sampled and attached to traces in the dashboard with <=1% additional latency overhead

Runbooks (quick reference)
- If p99 spike during chaos-lab:
  1. Run quick filter: slice telemetry by qualifier_id and experiment_label to isolate the change.
  2. Collect top 3 kernel traces and inspect queue-depth histograms.
  3. If one kernel is dominant, revert the kernel change to kernel-fallback profile and re-run the step.
- If canary induces elevated error-rate:
  1. Pause traffic ramp.
  2. Execute automated rollback (route traffic back to baseline revision).
  3. Capture full core dumps and attach to an incident ticket with replication script.

Release gating checklist (must be red/green before promoting to general release)
- [ ] Unit and integration CI: green
- [ ] Qualification lab run: documented and green with artifacts uploaded to /s3/qualifier/<qualifier_id>/
- [ ] Observability signals updated and dashboards created
- [ ] Regression prompt-set run: human-reviewed failures triaged
- [ ] Rollback playbook validated in staging
- [ ] Security review (if change touches data plane or auth paths)

Operational notes and common pitfalls
- Memory fragmentation: small kernel-side allocator changes can change high-water marks without changing average usage — always inspect allocator heatmaps.
- NVMe stalls: some lab simulations surface stalls only at longer run durations — include at least one 6-hour endurance run for storage-dependent changes.
- Telemetry overhead: adding fine-grained per-kernel counters can increase CPU load; qualify sampling rate before enabling in canary.

Appendix: example CLI snippets and reproducibility tips
- Launch local qualifying harness (Docker):
  - docker run --rm -e RK_QUAL_DEBUG=1 -v $(pwd)/bench:/bench redwood/runtime-qualifier:latest /bench/run --corpus small-chat --out /tmp/qual.csv
- Quick telemetry export (prometheus query example):
  - prometheus_query 'histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(request_latency_bucket{qualifier_id="Q-20260215"}[5m])) by (le))'
- Replaying production slice to replica cluster:
  1. Generate curated trace: tools/trace_slice --start=2026-02-01T00:00Z --duration=1h --pattern=mixed > /tmp/slice.avro
  2. Replay: bench/replay --target=chaos-qualifier --trace /tmp/slice.avro --rate 200rps
